right_elbow_flexion.source: Fleisig et al. 1995, J Biomech - Tennis serve elbow kinematics; reinforced by Elliott et al. 2003 Sports Med

left_elbow_flexion.source: POC default - non-dominant arm flexion during serve

right_shoulder_abduction.source: Chow et al. 2003 J Sports Sci - Shoulder abduction ~80-100 deg at cocking/contact in elite servers

right_knee_flexion.source: Fleisig et al. 1995; Bahamonde & Knudson 2003 - knee flexion ~130-160 deg during serve loading phase

left_knee_flexion.source: Estimated - front knee flexes during leg drive, similar range to rear knee

trunk_lateral_tilt.source: angle_between convention: angle at mid_spine (L_shoulder-mid-R_shoulder), ~170° when upright

hip_shoulder_separation.source: angle_between convention: angle at R_hip (L_hip-R_hip-R_shoulder), ~160° when aligned

wrist_extension.source: angle_between convention: angle at wrist (elbow-wrist-index), ~160° when extended

right_elbow_flexion.source: Elliott et al. 2003 Sports Med; Knudson 2006 - elbow more extended at contact than prep, ~120-150 deg

left_elbow_flexion.source: Estimated - non-dominant elbow assists with unit turn, more flexed during backswing

right_shoulder_abduction.source: Knudson 2006; Elliott et al. 2003 - shoulder abduction ~70-95 deg during forehand contact

left_shoulder_abduction.source: Estimated - non-dominant shoulder used for balance and rotation initiation

right_knee_flexion.source: Estimated from biomechanics literature - moderate knee flexion for ground strokes, ~140-165 deg

left_knee_flexion.source: Estimated - front leg slightly more flexed during weight transfer on forehand

hip_shoulder_separation.source: angle_between convention - more rotation in forehand

metadata.description: Expert tennis player joint angle baselines for technique comparison. Angles in degrees. Mean values represent typical elite player values at key stroke phases; std reflects normal inter-player and intra-player variation.

joint_conventions.hip_shoulder_separation: angle between hip and shoulder rotation planes

primary_references: Fleisig GS et al. (1995) Biomechanics of the shoulder during the tennis serve. J Biomech 28(8).

metadata.notes: Values marked 'Estimated from biomechanics literature' are informed approximations based on published ranges and expert consensus, not direct measurement. Serve values are more reliable than forehand due to more extensive motion capture research. Std values represent typical variation among competitive-level players.
